steps.title: Before you read: which explanation would you accept for a ban on desk drinks?
Four rules, no explanations
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 143 words

At a car factory near Turin, staff had to reverse into every parking space. Nobody was ever told why. It must have been a safety measure — most car-park accidents happen when people drive out at the end of a shift — though half the workforce insisted on a tidier explanation.

A software firm in Seattle stopped its staff leaving the building at midday. They can't have banned the lunch break itself; that would have been illegal. They may have needed someone at the phones.

A logistics company in the Gulf started work at half past five in the morning. In that climate it might have been simple sense; by ten o'clock the yard is unusable.

And one London office banned drinks at every desk, on every floor, overnight. Somebody must have spilt something expensive.

steps.title: What do the four cases have in common?
options: All four rules were later withdrawn.
In each case the reason was never explained to the people affected.
All four companies were taken to court.
steps.answer: In each case the reason was never explained to the people affected.
steps.why: The title says it: four rules, no explanations. Each paragraph offers a guess, not a fact.

steps.title: The minister's list
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 146 words

The rules leaked last month, and the minister has been criticized for every one of them. Her staff must stand when she enters. They cannot speak first. Nobody may use the corridor outside her office while she is eating.

She has been accused of running a nineteenth-century office. She might have expected that; what she can't have expected is how fast the list travelled. Somebody must have photographed it, and they can't have done it by accident.

Her defence is that the rules apply only to her own team, and that she can count on them to understand. Critics blame her for exposing junior staff to a working practice nobody would justify today. One asked whether refusing to stand would count against you at a review.

No harsh penalty has followed, and nobody has faced anything like a suspended sentence. The minister has simply stopped eating at her desk.

steps.why: 'The rules apply only to her own team, and… she can count on them to understand.'

steps.title: Certain, or only possible?
steps.sub: Decide how sure the writer is in each sentence from the two texts.

items.text: It must have been a safety measure
They can't have done it by accident

Somebody must have spilt something expensive

steps.title: Complete the summary of both texts.

items.after: have been about safety in the car park.

steps.title: Saying how sure you are about the past
steps.html:
The complete rule, then a large example bank, then a worked transformation.

When you work backwards from evidence, English marks how certain you are with a modal, not with an adverb. The structure is always the same: modal + have + past participle.

Must have = I am sure it happened. Can't have / couldn't have = I am sure it did not happen. Between them sit might have, may have and could have = it is possible.

The opposite of must have is can't have, not mustn't have. Mustn't is a prohibition and is not used for deduction.

For a state rather than an action, add been: It must have been a safety measure. For an ongoing action, use been + -ing: They must have been testing something.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Twelve sentences, all built on the two texts.

It must have been a safety measure.
Sure — the evidence points one way only.

They can't have banned the lunch break.
Sure it did not happen: it would be illegal.

They may have needed someone at the phones.
Possible, no more.

It might have been simple sense in that climate.
Possible; might and may are interchangeable here.

Somebody must have spilt something expensive.
An overnight ban is strong evidence.

She might have expected the criticism.
Possible.

She can't have expected it to travel so fast.
Sure it did not happen.

Somebody must have photographed the list.
It exists in public, so it was photographed.

They can't have done it by accident.
The negative deduction, not mustn't have done.

He could have resigned rather than been fired.
Could have = one possibility among several.

They must have been testing a new policy.
A past action still in progress at that time.

Nobody can have read the whole list in that time.
Can have appears in negatives and questions.

steps.title: Turning evidence into a deduction
steps.html:
1. The evidence: on Monday every desk in the building had a drink on it. On Tuesday drinks were banned everywhere.
  2. Decide how sure you are. A total ban overnight is strong evidence of a single incident, so this is certainty.
  3. Choose the modal: certainty about the past → must have.
  4. Build it: must + have + past participle. The action is spill, whose participle is spilt (or spilled): Somebody must have spilt something.
  5. Now test the opposite. Could a cleaner have asked for it? That is only possible, not certain, so: A cleaner might have asked for it. And what you are sure did not happen: They can't have decided it that morning — never mustn't have decided.

steps.title: You are going to explain an unexplained rule.
steps.sub: Choose the one you will write about.

options.label: A rule at a place you have worked
A rule at your school or university
A rule in a public building near you
One of the four rules from the first text

steps.title: Write your explanation.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Describe the rule, then give one deduction you are sure about, one you think is possible, and one thing you are sure is not the reason.
steps.html:
• Describe the rule and say that it was never explained.
  • Give the deduction you are most confident about, with <i>must have</i>.
  • Give a second, weaker possibility, with <i>might / may / could have</i>.
  • Rule one explanation out, with <i>can't have</i>, and say why.

Useful language

  • Nobody was ever told why …
  • It must have been … / They must have decided …
  • It might / may / could have been …
  • They can't have … , because …
  • The obvious explanation would be … , but that doesn't fit.
  • Whatever the reason, staff were never told.
steps.modelHtml:
The lift that stops at every floor

The lift in my first office was set to stop at every floor on the way down, whether or not anybody had called it. Nobody was ever told why, and the sign on the wall said only that the setting was permanent.

It must have been a decision taken after something went wrong, because the setting was changed overnight, and the maintenance company was in the building that week. It might also have been about the ground-floor security desk: stopping at every floor meant everyone passed the camera on level one.

What it can't have been is energy saving. The lift used more power, not less, and the building manager was criticized for the bills all year.

Three years later nobody has explained it, and the setting is still there.
